body.heading: The waggle dance
paragraphs: When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she flies home and dances on the honeycomb. Her pattern is a figure-eight with a straight, waggling run through the middle.

That straight run is a set of directions. Its angle, measured against gravity inside the dark hive, tells the other bees which way to fly relative to the Sun. Its length carries the distance: roughly speaking, each extra second of waggling means about another kilometre to travel.

body.heading: More than a dinner map
paragraphs: For food very close to home, bees use a simpler round dance that says, in effect, “it’s near — go and search”. The waggle dance is reserved for journeys worth describing precisely.

Bees even use the same dance language when the colony is choosing a new home, with scouts advertising candidate nest sites. The biologist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance in the twentieth century, work that later earned him a Nobel Prize.

body.heading: Teamwork without a manager
paragraphs: No bee is in charge of the colony’s foraging. Instead, hundreds of small reports come in, dancers compete for attention, and the hive’s effort flows toward the best sources.
It is a reminder that communication does not need words. Sometimes a well-drawn map — even one drawn in dance — is enough.

takeaway: A bee’s figure-eight dance encodes both direction and distance — a tiny map drawn in movement, in the dark, for an audience of sisters.
